I think a lot of people subdue the importance of the ray tracing aspect for real time rendering.... to this day it still is the most accurate method for rendering a 3D scene, rasterization use "cheats" to try and emulate a ray traced image, when you use ray tracing you don't need to cheat.

Someone had to kickstart this in the consumer space, so I think it's a really bold move by nVidia, they're taking risks, and we're already seeing all this backlash...

Ray tracing is so computationally expensive that they still can't use it for rendering the whole scene in games, and as an example render FARMS (a LOT of processing power, and a LOT more expensive than an RTX 20XX) making CGI movies usualy take minutes to render a single frame, so it's something really advanced they're putting on these boards (and remember that these RTX cores are rendering faster than 4 Voltas for a MUCH cheaper price)

I'm not saying they aren't greedy, but I'm saying that they're putting enough new features to justify a price rise, and as I said previously, real time ray tracing had to start at some point. There's also the tensor cores, which could be great for media playback (maybe the DLSS idea can be extrapolated to be used to upscale lower res video with an amazing quality?) ; there's also the GDDR6 memory, which probably isn't the cheapest thing either right now. The build quality is higher, better cooling...  there are a lot of nice things to consider...

As always, early adopters pay the price. If you're in it just for the games, I agree with the opinion that this isn't a recommended purchase. As everyone says "if you don't like it you just don't buy it".

I for myself am really excited by the possibilities these new technologies bring to the table, and wished I could buy one, but I can't afford it right now.

Still, I'm really glad with my 1080 and rasterized games look great already, so I can definitley wait for the next generation of RTX cards. By then a lot more of us will be able to reap the benefits of this first step, and in a more refined and knowledgeable way (the hardware will be better and the developers will have better ideas of how to use the possibilities of such hardware).

It's true, they're too expensive for the majority of gamers (myself included), and frankly I don't find them at all 'reasonable', but unfortunately it's logical. I don't think people realize the tremendous investments in R&D that these companies have to make to design new products, not to talk about the fact that an important part of the cost of a graphics card is the manufacturing cost of the GPU itself. In previous generations, Nvidia could take advantage of significantly improved production nodes to shrink the newer chips and lower the cost, but now with Turing the opposite is true: the 12nm node is barely an advance over 16nm, and with Turing's vastly increased transistor count the RTX 2080 is about 16% bigger than the GTX 1080 Ti and 74% bigger than the GTX 1080. It's literally impossible to make bigger chips that sell for the same price as the previous generation without hurting your own profits, so in order to keep them untouched the price needs to go up accordingly.
Again, looking back at my first 'high-end' 3D card bought 20 years ago for about 120€, I find the current prices almost surreal, because we use these things to play, but as an engineer/investor it makes all the sense in the world.
